maintenance_guide.summer: Prefers partial to full shade and rich, moist, organic loams; tolerates dry shade once established.
maintenance_guide.fall: Fern-like foliage remains attractive through summer and autumn.
maintenance_guide.winter: Semi-evergreen in mild winters; keep crown protected with light leaf litter.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide clumps in early autumn or early spring.

advisor_description:
An exquisitely delicate, hair-fine limestone sedge forming soft, misty emerald cushions of thread-like foliage resembling living moss or miniature fairy grass, topped in spring with tiny ivory flower spikes.

Growth Habit & Form: Forms slow-spreading, dense, tufted mats 4–8 inches tall and 6–12 inches wide.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Glade and rock matrix; companions include fragrant sumac, Missouri evening primrose, and prairie smoke.

Recommended Garden Settings: Limestone glades, rock garden crevices, dry alkaline shade, and shady stone steps.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
A dramatic, architectural prairie wonder producing bold rosettes of spiny, yucca-like blue-gray sword foliage, sending up stiff stalks topped in midsummer with unique, spherical, thistle-like white flower globes smelling of honey.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright architectural clump 3–4 ft tall and 1.5–2 ft wide with an immense, deep woody taproot.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Architectural prairie focal point; companions include rattlesnake master, big bluestem, and purple coneflower.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, prairie restorations, dry gravel gardens, and modern architectural plantings.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Wait until 50°F+ before cutting back dried stems. Yucca-like foliage emerges in May.
maintenance_guide.summer: Impervious to drought, heat, wind, and poor clay; requires full sun and zero fertilizer.
maintenance_guide.fall: Spherical seed globes turn gunmetal-gray and persist for months, adding incredible winter structure.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stiff stems and bristly flower globes catch winter frost and snow like botanical sculptures.
maintenance_guide.division: Deep woody taproot; DO NOT divide or transplant once established. Propagate by seed.

advisor_description:
A cheerful, dense shrub bursting with masses of bright butter-yellow 1-inch blossoms with prominent pom-poms of fuzzy golden stamens from July through September. Fine-textured blue-green foliage and peeling cinnamon-colored bark.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 3–5 ft tall and wide as a neat, dense, multi-stemmed rounded dome. Very compact and tidy.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Pollen factory for native bees; perfect structural front-of-border shrub alongside coneflowers and grasses.

Recommended Garden Settings: Formal native borders, foundation plantings, rock gardens, and low pollinator hedges.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
A stately, historic woodland and prairie perennial bearing five-petaled, greenish-white blossoms with prominent central green cones in early summer, followed by distinctive cylindrical, cottony thimble-like seed heads in autumn.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, branched perennial 2–3 ft tall and 1.5 ft wide with deeply lobed, textured foliage.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Woodland edge matrix perennial; pairs with wild columbine, little bluestem, and lanceleaf coreopsis.

Recommended Garden Settings: Open woodland savannas, prairie borders, dry-to-medium borders, and cottage gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
An exotic, jaw-dropping botanical marvel bearing 3-inch, intricately fringed lavender-and-white blossoms with radiating corona filaments like celestial clocks from July to September, followed by edible, fragrant green 'maypop' fruits.

Growth Habit & Form: Rapidly climbing herbaceous vine growing 10–20 ft by tendrils, dying completely to the ground in winter.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Sole primary larval host plant for the magnificent Variegated Fritillary butterfly; vigorous root runner.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sturdy trellises, sunny boundary fences, butterfly sanctuaries, and edible native gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: High Maintenance. Requires active moisture management or boundary containment to manage vigorous growth. Adhere to seasonal timing to maximize ecological benefits while containing spread.
maintenance_guide.spring: Emerges very late in spring (late May) from root crown; do not despair. Remove old dead vines.
maintenance_guide.summer: Vigorous root suckering; install root barriers or edge regularly if planted in tight formal beds.
maintenance_guide.fall: Harvest hollow green fruits when soft and fragrant; delicious tropical flavor for jams and drinks.
maintenance_guide.winter: Vines die completely back to the rootstock; heavily mulch root crown in zone 5/6 to prevent deep frost penetration.
maintenance_guide.division: Easily propagated by digging rooted underground runners in early spring.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
The premier native lawn alternative and shade groundcover, creating a soft, fine-textured, flowing emerald-green meadow that billows in the wind. Spreads by delicate creeping rhizomes into an unbroken living carpet.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 6–10 inches tall with a gracefully arching habit, forming a dense, weed-suppressing matrix.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Supreme shade matrix groundcover; interplants under oak canopies with spring ephemerals and ferns.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dry shade under mature trees, shady lawn replacement, woodland borders, and foundation paths.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Mow or shear back to 2 inches once in early spring (at 50°F+) before early spring flower spikes emerge.
maintenance_guide.summer: Highly drought tolerant once established; excels in dry, poor, rocky or sandy shade under trees.
maintenance_guide.fall: Foliage remains green late into autumn; catches falling tree leaves to create rich natural soil.
maintenance_guide.winter: Semi-evergreen in mild winters; provides critical winter cover for ground-foraging birds and insects.

advisor_description:
An iconic understory tree erupting in early spring with clusters of magenta-pink pea-like blossoms directly along bare branches and trunk, followed by heart-shaped leaves that turn canary yellow in fall, adorned with persistent papery seed pods.

Growth Habit & Form: Reaches 20–30 ft tall and 25–35 ft wide with graceful, spreading, multi-stemmed or single-trunk vase architecture. Moderately fast growing with deep fibrous roots.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Understory accent tree; integrates seamlessly at woodland margins or mixed pollinator borders with spring phlox, columbine, and carex groundcovers.

Recommended Garden Settings: Patio specimen, woodland understory, foundation corner accent, and pollinator hedgerow.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Prune out dead, crossing, or diseased twigs immediately after spring flowering completes to maintain open vase structure.
maintenance_guide.summer: Water moderately during extended dry spells, particularly in full sun exposures, to prevent leaf scorch and verticillium stress.
maintenance_guide.fall: Leave flattened seed pods on branches; they provide late-season food for Northern Bobwhites and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.winter: Delicate zig-zagging branch pattern provides handsome winter garden architecture.
maintenance_guide.division: Taprooted legume; do not divide. Plant containerized saplings into well-drained loams.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A durable, deep-rooted prairie native producing dense clusters of three-lobed, palm-like green leaves topped in June and July with cheerful, 2-inch bright golden-yellow daisy blossoms.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, colonial perennial 1.5–2.5 ft tall that spreads vigorously via creeping rhizomes to form a dense colony.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Competitive prairie matrix spreader; holds soil against weeds; pairs with switchgrass and big bluestem.

Recommended Garden Settings: Prairie restorations, sunny erosion control slopes, roadside meadows, and naturalized acreage.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back old stalks at 50°F+. Rhizomes emerge vigorously with spring warmth.
maintenance_guide.summer: Extremely drought and heat tolerant; thrives in poor, dry, sandy or rocky soils in full sun.
maintenance_guide.fall: Foliage turns warm reddish-bronze in late autumn.
maintenance_guide.winter: Dense root mat binds unstable hillside soils against winter erosion.
maintenance_guide.division: Vigorous spreader; dig and divide rhizome clumps in early spring if restricting spread.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A sturdy native tree opening spring with upright greenish-yellow flower clusters, followed by prickly husks containing mahogany-brown buckeye nuts with pale eyes. Foliage turns subtle pumpkin-orange to yellowish-red in late summer.

Growth Habit & Form: Reaches 30–50 ft with a rounded, symmetrical 30–40 ft crown. Features corky, light gray fissured bark.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Understory to mid-canopy tree; pairs well with oak overstory and spring ephemeral carpet.

Recommended Garden Settings: Woodland restoration, naturalized parks, large shade gardens, and riparian transition zones.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
A charming understory tree producing pendulous clusters of creamy-white bell-shaped flowers in spring, followed by curious papery, inflated lantern-like seed pods that rattle in the autumn wind.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 10–15 ft tall and wide, forming an upright, suckering, multi-stemmed small tree or large shrub with striped greenish-brown bark.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Understory thicket-former; excellent naturalizing companion under tall oaks and walnuts.

Recommended Garden Settings: Woodland restorations, shaded streambanks, ravine slopes, and native shade gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

A virtually indestructible native groundcover shrub bearing small yellow flower clusters in early spring before trifoliate aromatic leaves unfurl, followed by hairy red berries on female plants and a dazzling autumn display of crimson, orange, and amber foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Spreading, suckering shrub 2–6 ft tall and 6–10 ft wide; forms dense, weed-suppressing thickets that hold unstable soil.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Living green mulch and erosion controller; companion to little bluestem and leadplant on hot, dry banks.

Recommended Garden Settings: Erosion control slopes, highway banks, hellstrips, parking lot medians, and drought-tolerant borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
A premier 4-season native tree bearing flat-topped cymes of starry creamy-white blossoms in spring, glossy plum-like foliage that turns deep wine-red to purple in autumn, and edible blue-black berries that sweeten after frost.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 12–20 ft tall and 8–15 ft wide with a dense, rounded, rigid-branched architecture resembling a hawthorn or wild plum without thorns.

Sociability & Matrix Role: High-value structural layer; hosts spring azure butterflies and provides dense nesting cover for songbirds.

Recommended Garden Settings: Formal native borders, foundation corners, woodland edges, and wildlife hedgerows.

The premier native black-eyed susan producing an unending profusion of golden-orange daisy blossoms with dark chocolate-brown central cones from July through October, held above broad, dark green hairy basal leaves.

Growth Habit & Form: Forms a dense, spreading clump 2–3 ft tall and 2 ft wide, spreading gradually via creeping rhizomes.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Massing matrix workhorse; combines seamlessly with little bluestem, purple coneflower, and switchgrass.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, rain gardens, cottage beds, commercial landscapes, and pollinator meadows.

maintenance_guide.summary: Medium Maintenance. Benefits from targeted mid-season care (such as Chelsea chopping or occasional division) and spring cutback timing to sustain peak vigor and compact garden form.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back old dead stalks at 50°F+. Clear tattered leaves to allow fresh emerald basal rosettes room to expand.
maintenance_guide.summer: Very heat and drought tolerant once established; deadheading spent flowers prolongs bloom into autumn.
maintenance_guide.fall: Do NOT cut down in fall; dark brown seed cones feed flocks of American Goldfinches all winter.
maintenance_guide.winter: Architectural dark cones contrast strikingly against white snow.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide crowded root clumps every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigorous flowering.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A jaw-dropping limestone glade native producing sprawling stems with narrow, silvery-veined leaves and immense, 4–5 inch canary-yellow crepe-paper blossoms that open in late afternoon and emit a sweet fragrance, followed by winged 4-angled seed pods.

Growth Habit & Form: Prostrate, sprawling perennial 6–12 inches tall and 2–3 ft wide with a deep, drought-proof woody taproot.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Front-of-border glade showstopper; pairs with little bluestem, sideoats grama, and wild petunia.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny rock gardens, limestone glades, retaining wall spillers, curbside hellstrips, and gravel borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Trim back old dead runners in early spring at 50°F+; shoots emerge from the central woody crown.
maintenance_guide.summer: Virtually drought-proof; requires full sun and sharply drained, poor rocky or alkaline soil. Intolerant of wet clay.
maintenance_guide.fall: Enormous winged papery seed capsules turn bronze and make fantastic dried floral elements.
maintenance_guide.winter: Deep taproot survives sub-zero temperatures; foliage dies back cleanly.
maintenance_guide.division: Deep woody taproot; DO NOT divide or transplant once established. Propagate by seed.

advisor_description:
The queen of native prairie grasses, forming a lush, hair-like emerald fountain that sways softly in the wind. Late summer produces airy pinkish-copper flower panicles that hover like mist, releasing a delightful fragrance of hot buttered popcorn, coriander, and sunflower seeds. Turns brilliant pumpkin-orange in fall.

Growth Habit & Form: Dense, tight, non-invasive clumping habit 18–24 inches tall (foliage) and 2–3 ft tall in bloom, with a 2–3 ft graceful arching spread.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Essential matrix groundcover; the gold-standard 'green mulch' prairie companion that suppresses weeds without crowding neighbor perennials.

Recommended Garden Settings: Formal perennial borders, curbside hellstrips, modern matrix massings, rock gardens, and prairie restorations.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back dried foliage to 2–3 inches in early spring (at 50°F+) using sharp shears before new emerald shoots emerge. Highly fire-tolerant.
maintenance_guide.summer: Extremely drought-proof once established; needs full sun and good drainage. Requires zero supplemental fertilizer.
maintenance_guide.fall: Spectacular golden-orange to copper fall color holds well into late autumn. Nutrient-rich seeds feed winter sparrows and juncos.
maintenance_guide.winter: Pale straw-colored fountain catches snow and maintains clean, manicured shape all winter without flattening.
maintenance_guide.division: Slow-growing clump; rarely if ever needs division. Propagate by seed or divide large mature clumps in early spring.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
An award-winning shade and moisture shrub producing long, arching 4–6 inch cylindrical racemes of fragrant creamy-white blossoms in early summer. Dark green lustrous leaves turn spectacular long-lasting shades of crimson, purple, and scarlet in late autumn.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 3–5 ft tall and 4–6 ft wide with arching branches that spread gradually via underground root stolons.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Moisture-loving colonial shrub; companions include winterberry, wild hydrangea, and Pennsylvania sedge.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rain gardens, shaded foundation borders, stream banks, and wet woodland edges.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Prune immediately after flowering in early summer to shape or control spread. Blooms on old wood.
maintenance_guide.summer: Prefers moist, organic, slightly acidic soils; tolerates heavy wet clay and temporary standing water.
maintenance_guide.fall: Sensational autumn color holds on branches well into November and December.
maintenance_guide.winter: Slender arching reddish stems offer subtle color against winter snow.

advisor_description:
A charismatic native bunchgrass bearing arching flower stalks adorned with two-ranked oat-like spikelets that dangle gracefully along one side of the stem, displaying vivid purple and red-orange stamens. Turns warm golden-tan in fall.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, clump-forming grass 1.5–2.5 ft tall and 1–2 ft wide with rhizomatous tendencies that knit loose soils together.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Medium prairie matrix grass; companions include purple prairie clover, black-eyed susan, and pale purple coneflower.

Recommended Garden Settings: Erosion-prone hillsides, dry meadows, low-water borders, and native turf alternatives.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back to ground in early spring at 50°F+. Clean out thatch with a light rake.
maintenance_guide.summer: Exceptionally drought and heat hardy; thrives in poor, rocky, shallow limestone soils in full sun.
maintenance_guide.fall: Dangling oat-like seeds turn straw-yellow and supply food for foraging songbirds and small mammals.
maintenance_guide.winter: Graceful arching stems retain kinetic beauty throughout winter snows.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide in spring every 4–6 years if needed.

advisor_description:
The true tallgrass prairie alumroot, forming a neat, tidy basal mound of scalloped, heart-shaped green leaves with prominent veins, sending up wiry 1.5–2.5 ft spikes of tiny greenish-cream bell blossoms with protruding orange anthers in June.

Growth Habit & Form: Compact, tidy clump 1–2 ft tall and 1 ft wide with a non-invasive woody root crown.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Prairie matrix groundcover; companions include sideoats grama, prairie dropseed, and blue-eyed grass.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny prairie borders, limestone glades, rock gardens, path edging, and dry sunny slopes.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Trim tattered winter foliage at 50°F+; fresh scalloped leaves emerge rapidly from crown.
maintenance_guide.summer: Much more sun- and drought-tolerant than woodland heucheras; thrives in dry-to-medium prairie soils.
maintenance_guide.fall: Basal foliage turns attractive reddish-bronze in late fall.
maintenance_guide.winter: Semi-evergreen basal mound stays flat against soil, surviving freezing winter winds.

advisor_description:
A magnificent 4-season Missouri native perennial forming a dense, willow-like shrubby mound clothed in glossy, leathery dark green foliage. In May, branch tips bear clusters of starry porcelain-blue flowers, followed by sensational golden-yellow fall color.

Growth Habit & Form: Stately, rounded shrub-like clump 2–3 ft tall and wide with a deep, tenacious root crown.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Structural matrix perennial; combines with purple coneflower, switchgrass, and swamp milkweed.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rain gardens, bioswales, sunny perennial borders, stream banks, and cottage gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut stems back to 2 inches in early spring (at 50°F+). Shoots emerge like asparagus in April.
maintenance_guide.summer: Tolerates wet gravelly soils as well as baking summer drought; completely pest and disease free.
maintenance_guide.fall: Foliage turns luminous bright golden-yellow, lasting for weeks in October. Cylindrical seed pods stand erect.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stiff stems and upright seed pods provide clean winter structure.
maintenance_guide.division: Dense, woody root crown; divide rarely in early spring with a sharp spade.

advisor_description:
A refined 4-season small tree opening early spring with pendulous clouds of delicate, pure white 5-petaled flowers before leaves emerge. Followed by sweet, edible blueberry-like purple pomes in June, copper-red summer new growth, and fiery orange-scarlet fall foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Reaches 15–25 ft with a 15–20 ft vase-like spread. Often multi-stemmed with smooth, slate-gray bark etched with subtle charcoal fissures.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Refined structural layer; complements woodland edge perennials, spring bulbs, and turf transitions without casting heavy shade.

Recommended Garden Settings: Entryway gardens, bird sanctuary plantings, edible landscapes, and shaded woodland borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Prune only to shape immediately after flowering ends in May. Remove any weak water sprouts or damaged twigs.
maintenance_guide.summer: Edible June berries are ravenously harvested by cedar waxwings, robins, and gardeners. Minimal supplemental water once established.
maintenance_guide.fall: Brilliant orange and red autumn foliage drop cleanly; leaves decompose rapidly into rich leaf mold.
maintenance_guide.winter: Striking gray bark with ornamental vertical striping adds sophisticated winter interest.

advisor_description:
A handsome wetland sedge named for botanist Charles Short, bearing dense, upright cylindrical seed spikes that turn deep chocolate-brown in summer, held proudly above broad blue-green foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright clumping sedge 1.5–2.5 ft tall and 1.5 ft wide with strong root crowns.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Wetland matrix clumper; pairs with cardinal flower, swamp milkweed, and blue pickerel.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rain gardens, bioswales, marsh margins, stream banks, and wet meadows.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.fall: Dark chocolate seed spikes persist into autumn, providing food for rails, ducks, and sparrows.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stiff stems hold upright through early winter.

advisor_description:
A lovely, early-blooming native fleabane forming low, spreading rosettes of soft, hairy leaves topped in April and May with clusters of cheerful, daisy-like blossoms with dozens of fine lavender-to-white rays and golden centers.

Growth Habit & Form: Low, stoloniferous groundcover 6–12 inches tall spreading to form dense, weed-suppressing carpets.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Living green mulch; carpets soil in dappled shade or sun; companions include woodland phlox and sedges.

Recommended Garden Settings: Woodland edge borders, dappled shade paths, dry-to-moist slopes, and naturalized shade gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

An extraordinarily prolific, long-blooming native producing silky, 3-inch bowl-shaped blossoms of delicate pastel pink to translucent white with yellow throats from May to July, held above narrow, toothed lanceolate foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Vigorous, spreading colonial groundcover 1–1.5 ft tall, spreading rapidly via vigorous underground rhizomes.

Sociability & Matrix Role: High-vigor colonial spreader; best in enclosed beds or wild prairie expanses; will overrun slow, polite clumpers in formal borders.

Recommended Garden Settings: Erosion-prone sunny slopes, curbside hellstrips, enclosed raised beds, highway banks, and naturalized meadows.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
An exquisitely sculptural native tree boasting horizontal, tiered branches that float in tiered architectural pagoda layers. Fragrant yellowish-white flower clusters in late spring produce dark blue berries on showy red stems, ending in reddish-purple fall color.

Growth Habit & Form: Reaches 15–25 ft tall and wide with a horizontal, spreading pagoda habit. Unlike other dogwoods, leaves are arranged alternately along green branches.

Sociability & Matrix Role: High-end focal point for shaded settings; companions include wild hydrangea, columbine, and woodland phlox.

Recommended Garden Settings: Woodland edge focal point, northeast house corners, contemplative shade gardens, and bird borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

A charming, tough woodland aster bearing loose, frothy clouds of starry white blossoms with yellow centers that mature to purplish-red in August and September, held on distinctive zig-zagging dark mahogany-black wiry stems.

Growth Habit & Form: Spreading, mounding clump 1.5–2.5 ft tall and 2 ft wide with coarsely toothed, heart-shaped basal leaves.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Dry shade matrix workhorse; completely illuminates dark woodland corners; pairs with carex and Christmas fern.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dry shade under mature deciduous trees, woodland borders, shaded slopes, and naturalized woods.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
An architectural perennial acting like a woody shrub, producing breathtaking 12–18 inch spires of intense indigo-blue lupine-like blossoms in late spring above handsome clover-like blue-green foliage. Flowers give way to inflated charcoal-black seed pods that rattle in autumn.

Growth Habit & Form: Forms a dense, rounded shrub-like mound 3–4 ft tall and wide with an exceptionally deep, drought-proof taproot.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Structural keystone perennial; pairs with pale purple coneflower, prairie dropseed, and butterfly weed.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, cottage gardens, prairie meadows, and low-maintenance foundation plantings.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Wait until 50°F+ before cutting back dried stems. Shoots emerge like purple asparagus in April. No staking needed.
maintenance_guide.summer: Virtually drought-proof once taproot is established; thrives in heat, humidity, and poor clay soils.
maintenance_guide.fall: Leave decorative charcoal seed pods standing on the bush; pods rattle like castanets in the autumn wind.
maintenance_guide.winter: Dried shrubby architecture breaks off at ground level in late winter like a prairie tumbleweed if unpruned.
maintenance_guide.division: Deep woody taproot; DO NOT divide or transplant once established. Propagate by seed.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A handsome architectural woodland perennial featuring broad, oval, chevron-patterned green leaves, sending up long, airy, wiry 2–3 ft wands studded with tiny, jewel-like crimson-red florets from July through October.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, arching clump 2–3 ft tall and 2 ft wide with fibrous root crowns. Seeds 'jump' when touched.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Shade matrix filler; textured foliage pairs with maidenhair fern, wild ginger, and woodland phlox.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dappled shade gardens, woodland borders, shaded moist swales, and native cottage borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back old wiry stalks at 50°F+; fresh patterned foliage emerges in April.
maintenance_guide.summer: Prefers moist, rich, organic soils in partial to full shade; tolerates average garden soil.
maintenance_guide.fall: Seed wands turn bronze-tan; ripe seeds snap explosively ('jump') several feet when brushed.
maintenance_guide.winter: Dormant crowns survive deep winter cold under fallen leaf litter.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide root clumps in spring; thin volunteer seedlings if needed.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
An iconic native harbinger of spring bearing nodding, bicolored bell blossoms with flaring scarlet-red spurs and glowing yellow corollas in April and May, held above delicate, ferny blue-green columbine foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Airy, upright clump 1.5–2.5 ft tall and 1–1.5 ft wide with fibrous roots and short taproot.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Premier early spring hummingbird magnet; pairs with woodland phlox, bluebells, and Christmas fern.

Recommended Garden Settings: Woodland gardens, shaded rocky slopes, dappled borders, limestone outcroppings, and hummingbird beds.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Blossoms open precisely as Ruby-throated Hummingbirds return; avoid cutting foliage until bloom finishes.
maintenance_guide.summer: Thrives in dappled shade to full sun; handles rocky, alkaline, thin soils. Leaf miner damage is cosmetic and non-lethal.
maintenance_guide.fall: Papery upright seed pods split to release shiny black seeds; self-seeds politely in rock crevices.
maintenance_guide.winter: Semi-evergreen basal foliage hugs the ground in mild winters.
maintenance_guide.division: Short-lived perennial that renews reliably by seed; do not divide established taproots.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A beloved woodland treasure forming fragrant carpets of soft lavender-blue to violet five-petaled blossoms with notched petals in April and May, filling the spring forest floor with a heavenly sweet perfume.

Growth Habit & Form: Spreading, semi-evergreen clump 10–14 inches tall and 12–18 inches wide, creeping via surface runners.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Classic spring woodland matrix groundcover; companions include columbine, wild geranium, and ferns.

Recommended Garden Settings: Deciduous shade gardens, woodland paths, dappled foundation borders, and spring bulb beds.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Trim lightly after spring flowering to tidy foliage and stimulate dense, weed-choking groundcover mats.
maintenance_guide.summer: Prefers rich, moist, organic woodland soil in dappled shade; drought tolerant once established.
maintenance_guide.fall: Creeping surface stems establish roots to expand the colony.
maintenance_guide.winter: Semi-evergreen basal foliage stays green beneath fallen autumn leaves.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide rooted creeping stems in spring or autumn.

advisor_description:
The beloved native purple coneflower bearing large, showy daisy blossoms with reflexed rose-purple ray petals surrounding an architectural, spiky coppery-orange central cone from June through August, borne on stout, rough-hairy stems.

Growth Habit & Form: Stout, upright clump 2–4 ft tall and 1.5–2 ft wide with a deep, drought-proof fibrous-taproot crown.

Sociability & Matrix Role: The gold-standard pollinator and bird keystone; pairs with little bluestem, black-eyed susans, and prairie dropseed.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, prairie meadows, pollinator beds, cottage gardens, and cutting borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back dried stalks at 50°F+, leaving 8–12 inches for stem-nesting bees. Shoots emerge in late April.
maintenance_guide.summer: Extremely drought, heat, and clay tolerant; requires full sun. Avoid excessive fertilizer which causes weak stems.
maintenance_guide.fall: Do NOT deadhead in autumn; leave spiky cones standing. Cones feed American Goldfinches all winter.
maintenance_guide.winter: Architectural blackened cones stand tall above snowdrifts, providing striking winter focal interest.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide mature multi-crowned clumps in early spring every 4–5 years.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A delicate, feathery native perennial bearing needle-like, soft fringed foliage that forms an airy, cloud-like mound. Starry porcelain-blue blossoms cluster at stem tips in May, followed in autumn by a jaw-dropping blaze of golden-yellow foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Bushy, rounded mound 2–3 ft tall and wide with deep fibrous roots and non-aggressive clump habit.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Textural matrix perennial; pairs with butterfly weed, purple prairie clover, and sideoats grama.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dry sunny borders, rock gardens, limestone glades, prairie restorations, and autumn showcase beds.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back dead stems to ground level in early spring at 50°F+; fresh feathery shoots emerge in April.
maintenance_guide.summer: Impervious to drought, intense heat, and poor rocky soils; requires full sun for best golden fall foliage.
maintenance_guide.fall: Foliage turns electric butter-yellow and amber, persisting for nearly a month in autumn.
maintenance_guide.winter: Slender upright stems hold decorative cylindrical seed pods.
maintenance_guide.division: Slow-growing clump; rarely needs division. Divide large crowns in early spring.

advisor_description:
An exceptionally tidy, well-behaved early-blooming native beebalm producing dense, rounded terminal heads of pale pink to white two-lipped blossoms speckled with purple dots in May and June. Aromatic, dark green foliage turns wine-red in autumn.

Growth Habit & Form: Compact, bushy clump 1.5–2 ft tall and wide. Unlike wild bergamot, it forms a tight clump that does not run aggressively.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Early-season bumblebee and hummingbird magnet; superb mildew resistance; pairs with lanceleaf coreopsis.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny borders, dry-to-medium woodland edges, pollinator beds, and cottage gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back old stems at 50°F+, leaving 8–12 inches for stem-nesting bees. Foliage emerges early with purple tints.
maintenance_guide.summer: Remarkably drought and powdery mildew resistant compared to other monardas; thrives in sun or partial shade.
maintenance_guide.fall: Foliage takes on rich burgundy-purple autumn color; dried spherical seed heads persist.
maintenance_guide.winter: Aromatic dried seed heads smell of oregano; basal rosette overwinters semi-evergreen.

advisor_description:
A showy, ultra-reliable native perennial producing erect wands of tubular, two-lipped white to pale lavender-pink bell blossoms in May and June, rising above lustrous, semi-evergreen dark green to bronze-tinted basal foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, columnar clump 2–3 ft tall and 1.5 ft wide with fibrous roots and stout flower stems.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Early summer pollinator engine; pairs with purple coneflower, butterfly weed, and blue-eyed grass.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, prairie meadows, rain gardens, cottage beds, and pollinator plantings.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back dried stalks at 50°F+, leaving 8–12 inches of stubble for solitary bee nesting.
maintenance_guide.summer: Highly adaptable to both baking summer drought and wet spring clay; very pest and disease free.
maintenance_guide.fall: Woody, copper-colored seed capsules turn dark chocolate in fall and feed overwintering birds.
maintenance_guide.winter: Semi-evergreen basal foliage takes on rich reddish-purple winter hues.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide root clumps every 3 years in early spring to maintain vigor.

advisor_description:
An architectural woodland cool-season grass featuring distinctive, bristly horizontal flower spikes that look exactly like antique bottle brushes, held perpendicular to graceful arching green stems from June to August.

Growth Habit & Form: Clump-forming bunchgrass 2–3 ft tall and 1–1.5 ft wide, adapted specifically to dappled woodland light.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Cool-season woodland matrix grass; pairs with woodland phlox, columbine, and zig-zag goldenrod.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dry-to-moist woodland edges, shady savanna restorations, native woodland borders, and bird gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back old foliage in late winter before early spring green-up begins. Greens up early in cool weather.
maintenance_guide.summer: Prefers partial to dappled shade; drought tolerant under mature tree canopies.
maintenance_guide.fall: Bristly seed spikes mature to wheat-tan and drop seeds to regenerate naturally.
maintenance_guide.winter: Fine, light straw-colored silhouettes provide subtle texture in winter woods.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide dormant clumps in early spring or early fall.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
Dazzling early spring display of intensely fragrant snowy-white blossoms enveloping thorny branches before foliage, followed by succulent yellow-to-crimson native plums that make delectable preserves, ending in golden-orange fall foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 15–25 ft tall and wide; thorny, multi-branched small tree that naturalizes into impenetrable thickets via root suckers.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Structural keystone and nesting cover; companion to prairie grasses and woodland edge borders.

Recommended Garden Settings: Pollinator sanctuaries, shelterbelts, perimeter privacy thickets, and native fruit orchards.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Medium Maintenance. Benefits from targeted mid-season care (such as Chelsea chopping or occasional division) and spring cutback timing to sustain peak vigor and compact garden form.
maintenance_guide.spring: Prune out crossing branches and water suckers after bloom to maintain airflow. Thin thickets if boundary spread is restricted.
maintenance_guide.summer: Plums swell in July and August; provide moderate moisture to maximize fruit plumpness. Highly resilient to heat.
maintenance_guide.fall: Collect fallen plums for homemade jam or leave for wildlife. Rake mummified fruits to avoid brown rot.
maintenance_guide.winter: Thorny, dense branch tangle provides essential winter windbreak and predator defense for native songbirds.
maintenance_guide.division: Sprouts vigorously from roots; sever and transplant dormant root suckers in late autumn or early spring.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A majestic tallgrass prairie cornerstone with striking vertical blue-green foliage, bursting in late summer with magnificent, plume-like copper-bronze flower panicles studded with bright yellow stamens that sparkle in the autumn sun.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, clump-forming grass 3–6 ft tall and 2–3 ft wide with strong, wind-firm stems.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Tallgrass structural keystone; companions include compass plant, prairie dock, and New England aster.

Recommended Garden Settings: Prairie meadows, large perennial borders, highway banks, and wildlife habitat corridors.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back to 3 inches in late spring (at 50°F+). Takes off rapidly with summer warmth.
maintenance_guide.summer: Extremely drought and heat tolerant; thrives in clay, loam, and dry soils. Avoid excessive fertilizer.
maintenance_guide.fall: Sensational burnished bronze and golden fall color; prolific seed producer for songbirds.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stout stems stand erect through the winter, providing critical thermal cover for quail and wildlife.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide dormant clumps in spring with a sharp spade.

advisor_description:
A refined native woodland alumroot forming compact mounds of scalloped, heart-shaped green leaves exquisitely marbled with silver, pewter, and burgundy veining, sending up wiry 2–3 ft wands of tiny greenish-white bell blossoms in June.

Growth Habit & Form: Compact, mounding semi-evergreen clump 1–2 ft tall and 1–1.5 ft wide with a woody rootstock.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Foliage matrix groundcover; companions include wild columbine, wild ginger, and maidenhair fern.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dappled shade borders, shaded rock gardens, path edging, north foundation beds, and container planters.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Thrives in well-drained, organically rich woodland soils in partial to full shade; drought tolerant once rooted.
maintenance_guide.fall: Marbled foliage intensifies with rich purple-red veining as autumn temperatures drop.
maintenance_guide.winter: Evergreen to semi-evergreen rosette provides subtle winter texture.

advisor_description:
Missouri native winter marvel blooming in late winter (January–March) during mild thaws with spicy-fragrant, spidery copper-red to golden-yellow blossoms whose ribbon petals curl in freezing cold and unfurl in sunshine. Brilliant yellow-orange fall foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Spreading multi-stemmed shrub 6–10 ft tall and 8–12 ft wide, forming colonial thickets along waterways.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Winter accent and stream stabilizer; pairs with winterberry, silky dogwood, and sedges in wet soils.

Recommended Garden Settings: Bioswales, rain gardens, creek bank stabilization, and winter viewing gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
A valuable wetland dogwood bearing flat-topped clusters of creamy-white spring blossoms, followed by porcelain blue-and-white berries in late summer, reddish-purple autumn foliage, and deep burgundy-red winter twigs.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 6–10 ft tall and wide, forming a spreading, rounded multi-stemmed thicket whose lower branches root where they touch soil.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Soil-stabilizing thicket former; combines with buttonbush, elderberry, and swamp milkweed.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rain gardens, creek banks, bioswales, stormwater detention basins, and wildlife hedgerows.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Prune back one-third of oldest stems to ground level every 2–3 years in early spring to encourage bright red new canes.
maintenance_guide.summer: Prefers wet to moist soils; tolerates seasonal inundation and heavy, poorly drained clay.
maintenance_guide.fall: Showy pale blue drupes are quickly eaten by wood ducks, grouse, and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.winter: Burgundy winter stems create vibrant contrast against winter snowscapes.
maintenance_guide.division: Branches naturally layer where touching soil; sever and transplant rooted canes in early spring.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A vigorous woody climbing vine bearing abundant clusters of trumpet-shaped, reddish-orange flowers with bright yellow throats in late spring that emit a delicate mocha-chocolate fragrance. Lustrous leathery leaves turn reddish-purple in winter.

Growth Habit & Form: High-climbing woody vine climbing 30–50 ft by tendrils with adhesive pads that cling directly to brick and bark.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Vertical hummingbird magnet; covers arbors, fences, and walls without choking mature trees.

Recommended Garden Settings: Trellises, brick walls, sturdy arbors, chain link fence covers, and wildlife borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Medium Maintenance. Benefits from targeted mid-season care (such as Chelsea chopping or occasional division) and spring cutback timing to sustain peak vigor and compact garden form.
maintenance_guide.spring: Prune immediately after late-spring flowering to shape or control vine spread. Blooms on old wood.
maintenance_guide.summer: Enjoys moist, rich, well-drained soils in full sun to partial shade; highly heat tolerant.
maintenance_guide.fall: Long, flat seed pods develop and persist into winter.
maintenance_guide.winter: Foliage is semi-evergreen in the Kansas City zone, turning rich purple-bronze in winter.
maintenance_guide.division: Propagate by softwood cuttings in summer or layering stems.

advisor_description:
A dazzling late-summer native producing frothy, powder-puff clusters of vivid ageratum-like mist-blue to lavender-blue blossoms from July through October that blanket the garden in cool blue clouds, buzzing with butterflies.

Growth Habit & Form: Spreading, multi-stemmed perennial 1.5–3 ft tall that spreads vigorously via shallow underground creeping rhizomes.

Sociability & Matrix Role: High-vigor colonial spreader; excellent for rain gardens and large meadow matrices; may overtake slow companions in small beds.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rain gardens, bioswales, stream banks, moist sunny borders, and naturalized butterfly gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Medium Maintenance. Benefits from targeted mid-season care (such as Chelsea chopping or occasional division) and spring cutback timing to sustain peak vigor and compact garden form.
maintenance_guide.spring: Emerges late in spring (May); cut back old stems at 50°F+. Edge boundaries if containing within formal beds.
maintenance_guide.summer: Enjoys rich, moist to wet soils in full sun to partial shade; tolerates temporary flooding.
maintenance_guide.fall: Breathtaking blue floral clouds provide vital late-season fuel for migrating monarchs.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stems die back cleanly; creeping rhizomes survive cold winters under snow.
maintenance_guide.division: Easily divided by digging and transplanting rooted runners in spring or autumn.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
The electrifying 'Fire Pink' producing loose clusters of star-shaped, five-petaled blossoms of the most intense, glowing scarlet-red with deeply notched petal tips from April to June, rising above sticky-haired green stems.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, airy clump 12–18 inches tall and 12 inches wide with a taproot-like woody rootstock.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Spring hummingbird beacon; glowing red accents among woodland companions like wild columbine and ferns.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rocky woodland slopes, shaded rock gardens, well-drained dappled borders, and hummingbird gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Blossoms open in mid-spring; sticky stems naturally trap small crawling insects (hence 'catchfly').
maintenance_guide.summer: Requires sharp drainage and dappled light; highly intolerant of heavy, soggy, waterlogged clay.
maintenance_guide.fall: Seed capsules split to disperse seeds; basal rosette hugs the ground.
maintenance_guide.winter: Basal foliage overwinters semi-evergreen; needs dry winter soil conditions to prevent crown rot.
maintenance_guide.division: Short-lived perennial that self-sows gently; propagate by fresh seed.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A timeless architectural woodland native featuring graceful, arching unbranched stems clothed in alternate, ribbed green leaves. In May, pairs of pendulous, greenish-white bell-shaped blossoms dangle beneath the arching stems, followed by blue-black berries in fall.

Growth Habit & Form: Graceful arching clump 2–4 ft tall and 2 ft wide, spreading slowly into majestic colonies via thick, jointed rhizomes.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Structural shade matrix anchor; companions include Christmas fern, wild ginger, and black cohosh.

Recommended Garden Settings: Shaded woodland borders, north-facing slopes, foundation shade beds, and native shade gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Shoots pierce the earth like spears in April; clear heavy matted debris at 50°F+.
maintenance_guide.summer: Thrives in rich, moist, organic soils in partial to full shade; remarkably drought tolerant once established.
maintenance_guide.fall: Berries ripen to deep blue-black; foliage turns glorious clear butter-yellow in October.
maintenance_guide.winter: Leaves and stems drop cleanly, leaving distinctive round circular scars ('Solomon's seals') on rhizomes.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide thick jointed rhizomes in late summer or early autumn every 4–6 years.

advisor_description:
A beloved shade-tolerant grass resembling bamboo, bearing drooping, flattened oat-like seed heads that dangle gracefully from arching stems like shimmering river jewelry. Translucent seedheads flutter in the breeze and turn rich copper-bronze in fall.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, arching clump 2–4 ft tall and 1.5–2.5 ft wide. Spreads moderately by short rhizomes and self-seeding.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Shade matrix grass; combines beautifully with wild hydrangeas, woodland phlox, and ferns.

Recommended Garden Settings: Shady borders, rain gardens, woodland stream banks, erosion slopes, and dry shade under trees.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back dried stems to 2 inches in spring (50°F+). Remove unwanted seedlings if spread is contained.
maintenance_guide.summer: Thrives in partial to full shade and moist-to-medium soil; tolerates dry shade once established.
maintenance_guide.fall: Copper seedheads are magnificent in autumn arrangements and feed Northern Cardinals and buntings.
maintenance_guide.winter: Bronze seed tassels rustle pleasantly in winter wind and catch frosted snow.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide clumps in early spring; pull unwanted volunteer seedlings.

advisor_description:
A vigorous, beautiful native groundcover producing deeply lobed, toothed dark green foliage topped from May to July with abundant, pure snowy-white 5-petaled blossoms with sunny yellow centers.

Growth Habit & Form: Vigorous, spreading colonial groundcover 1–2 ft tall, spreading aggressively by creeping underground rhizomes.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Competitive colonizer; ideal for expansive wet slopes or erosion control; will quickly overrun small polite perennials in tight borders.

Recommended Garden Settings: Erosion-prone stream banks, wet drainage ditches, rain gardens, naturalized meadows, and woodland edges.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Shoots emerge vigorously in spring; cut back old growth at 50°F+. Install root barriers in small garden settings.
maintenance_guide.summer: Thrives in moist, wet, organic soils in sun or partial shade; drought-tolerant once dense mat forms.
maintenance_guide.fall: Dense foliage mat blankets soil, preventing weed seed germination.
maintenance_guide.winter: Creeping rhizomes overwinter with complete cold hardiness.
maintenance_guide.division: Easily divided by digging and dividing rooted rhizomes in spring or autumn.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
The classic, sun-loving native tickseed bearing abundant bright golden-yellow daisy blossoms with toothed, frilled petal tips from May to July, dancing on slender wiry stems above lance-shaped basal leaves.

Growth Habit & Form: Clump-forming perennial 1.5–2.5 ft tall and 1.5 ft wide with fibrous roots.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Sunny pollinator matrix workhorse; companions include purple coneflower, blue-eyed grass, and little bluestem.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, prairie meadows, rock gardens, curbside hellstrips, and roadside banks.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back previous year's dead stems at 50°F+; fresh green basal leaves emerge early.
maintenance_guide.summer: Extremely drought and heat tolerant; thrives in poor, rocky, sandy, or clay soils in full sun. Deadhead for rebloom.
maintenance_guide.fall: Seed heads feed goldfinches and native sparrows; self-seeds politely in open soil.
maintenance_guide.winter: Basal leaf rosette stays semi-evergreen through winter.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide root clumps every 2–3 years in early spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

advisor_description:
An ethereal, miniature woodland spring jewel bearing delicate, columbine-like lacy foliage topped in April and May with solitary or small clusters of starry, pure white to pale pink blossoms with yellow stamens.

Growth Habit & Form: Delicate, compact clump 4–8 inches tall and 6 inches wide arising from small, tuberous cluster roots.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Spring woodland matrix jewel; companions include wild ginger, dwarf crested iris, and maidenhair fern.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rich woodland shade gardens, shaded rock gardens, mossy path edges, and native miniature gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
An eye-catching native producing radiating daisy blossoms of fiery red-orange petals tipped with bright sunshine-yellow, surrounding a dark burgundy-red central button from May through frost.

Growth Habit & Form: Bushy, multi-branched mound 1–2 ft tall and 1–1.5 ft wide with hairy, dandelion-like leaves.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Hot-color accent and long-season pollinator magnet; pairs with blue grama, sideoats grama, and wild petunia.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny rock gardens, limestone glades, curbside hellstrips, dry sunny borders, and container plantings.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Impervious to intense heat, drought, and poor, baking rocky soils; requires full sun and sharp drainage.
maintenance_guide.fall: Blooms continuously until hard frost. Spherical fuzzy seed heads drop seeds to self-sow reliably.

advisor_description:
The classic Missouri state tree featuring large, snowy white petal-like bracts that carpet the forest understory in April before foliage. Scarlet-red autumn foliage is accompanied by glossy bright red berries that glisten against alligator bark.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 15–25 ft tall and wide with a flat-topped to rounded pyramidal crown and graceful horizontal branching.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Cherished woodland understory tree; pairs with serviceberry, redbud, and woodland phlox in partial shade.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dappled shade lawns, woodland clearings, sheltered foundation beds, and bird habitat gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Prune out dead wood after spring bloom. Ensure good air movement around canopy to prevent foliar fungal blights.
maintenance_guide.summer: Mulch root zone generously; provide deep watering during prolonged summer droughts to avoid leaf scorch.
maintenance_guide.fall: Scarlet berries provide high-fat fuel for autumn songbird migrations. Leaves drop to form nutrient-rich humus.
maintenance_guide.winter: Flattened biscuit-shaped flower buds sit prominently on twig tips all winter.
maintenance_guide.division: Do not divide. Plant container-grown saplings in rich, acidic to neutral, well-drained soil.

advisor_description:
A rare, delicate Missouri glade native vine bearing exquisite, nodding, thick-walled urn-shaped or bell-shaped blossoms of soft lavender-pink to pale purplish-white with pale yellow margins, followed by fluffy, silvery plumed seed heads.

Growth Habit & Form: Slender, non-aggressive climbing vine 6–12 ft tall that climbs gently by twisting leaf petioles.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Gentle native climber; scrambles harmlessly over native shrubs like aromatic sumac or through trellises.

Recommended Garden Settings: Limestone glade borders, sunny rock gardens, decorative trellises, and native shrub companions.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Prefers 'head in the sun, roots in the shade'; needs well-drained, alkaline limestone soil.
maintenance_guide.fall: Silvery, feathery seed tails catch the autumn sunlight like shimmering stars.

advisor_description:
A wonderful, velvety evergreen groundcover forming dense, weed-suppressing carpets of broad, paddle-shaped silvery-gray leaves, sending up 8–12 inch fuzzy stems in April and May topped with curious fuzzy white flower heads resembling kitten paws.

Growth Habit & Form: Low, mat-forming stoloniferous groundcover 2–4 inches tall (foliage) and 8–12 inches in bloom, spreading via leafy runners.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Sole primary larval host plant for the American Lady butterfly; companions include prairie dropseed and wild petunia.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dry sunny slopes, rock gardens, curbside hellstrips, glade borders, and path edging.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Pussy-toe flower stalks emerge early; caterpillars of American Lady butterflies web leaves into larval shelters.
maintenance_guide.summer: Exceptional drought, heat, and poor-soil tolerance; excels in baking, rocky, dry clay where lawn grass dies.
maintenance_guide.fall: Silvery foliage forms a tight, weed-proof mat that catches low autumn light.
maintenance_guide.winter: Evergreen silvery foliage provides year-round groundcover and winter soil erosion control.
maintenance_guide.division: Easily divided by digging rooted stolon runners in spring or autumn.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
An elegant large shrub or small tree bearing large flat creamy-white flower clusters in May, finely serrated lustrous foliage that turns brilliant red-purple in autumn, and hanging clusters of edible sweet blue-black berries that shrivel like sweet raisins.

Growth Habit & Form: Reaches 15–20 ft tall and 8–12 ft wide with an upright, arching vase habit, forming suckering thickets if untamed.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Wildlife hedgerow structural anchor; pairs with serviceberries, dogwoods, and woodland border perennials.

Recommended Garden Settings: Woodland margins, screening hedges, moist swale banks, and wildlife habitat corridors.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Tolerates clay, alkaline soil, and full sun to partial shade; minimal irrigation needed once established.
maintenance_guide.fall: Berries sweeten after light frost; delicious eaten straight from the bush or left for cedar waxwings.
maintenance_guide.winter: Long, pointed terminal flower buds resemble heron beaks and add distinct winter curiosity.

advisor_description:
An all-season prairie showstopper with fine blue-green to silver foliage that transforms in autumn into an electric blaze of copper, amber, burgundy, and plum. Fluffy, silver-white seedheads sparkle in backlighting like crystalline plumes.

Growth Habit & Form: Tight, upright vertical bunchgrass 2–3 ft tall and 12–18 inches wide with deep, fibrous roots that reach up to 5 feet into dry subsoil.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Pivotal matrix structural grass; pairs exquisitely with purple coneflower, butterfly weed, and aromatic aster.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny borders, dry prairie meadows, rock gardens, erosion slopes, and curbside hellstrips.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back to 2 inches above ground in late spring (at 50°F+). Warm-season grass that wakes up as soil warms in May.
maintenance_guide.summer: Requires full sun and lean, dry-to-medium soils. Excess fertilizer or overly rich soil causes stems to flop.
maintenance_guide.fall: Sensational copper-red autumn color and silvery seed plumes. Stems remain upright through wind and rain.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stiff stems and fluffy seedheads provide essential winter food and shelter for juncos, finches, and skipper butterfly larvae.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide dormant clumps in early spring just as green growth initiates if center thins after 5–7 years.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
The legendary 'Wild Bergamot' producing magnificent, mop-like terminal flower heads of lavender-pink tubular blossoms from July to September that emit an intoxicating spicy oregano-thyme aroma, swarming with bees, clearwing moths, and butterflies.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, branched clump 3–4 ft tall and 2–3 ft wide that spreads steadily via underground creeping rhizomes.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Premier pollinator powerhouse; companions include yellow coneflower, switchgrass, and big bluestem.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, prairie meadows, rain garden slopes, and naturalized pollinator plantings.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Medium Maintenance. Benefits from targeted mid-season care (such as Chelsea chopping or occasional division) and spring cutback timing to sustain peak vigor and compact garden form.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back old stalks at 50°F+, leaving 12 inches for stem-nesting bees. Pinch stems in late May for bushier habit.
maintenance_guide.summer: Highly drought tolerant once established; enjoys full sun and good air circulation to minimize powdery mildew.
maintenance_guide.fall: Dried button-like seed heads persist into autumn; aromatic seeds feed winter songbirds.
maintenance_guide.winter: Fragrant dried calyx buttons provide winter architectural interest and shelter beneficial insects.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide spreading root clumps every 3 years in early spring to control spread and maintain center vigor.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
Known as Musclewood or Ironwood for its uniquely fluted, muscular, smooth blue-gray trunk resembling sinewy flexed muscle. Drooping catkins accompany new leaves, maturing into papery 3-lobed leafy bracts holding seeds, while fall foliage blazes yellow, orange, and scarlet.

Growth Habit & Form: Slow-growing understory tree 20–35 ft tall and 20–30 ft wide with a dense, rounded, spreading umbrella crown.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Structural understory anchor; tolerates deep shade, seasonal flooding, and urban clay compaction.

Recommended Garden Settings: Shaded courtyards, rain gardens, heavy clay borders, stream margins, and naturalized woods.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Highly adaptable to heavy clay and standing water; requires minimal attention once established.

advisor_description:
An extraordinary, sculptural sedge bearing dramatic, 1.5-inch starburst seed heads that look like antique medieval morning stars or miniature spiky maces, floating above lustrous wide green foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, arching clump 2–3 ft tall and 1.5–2 ft wide with an exotic, architectural presence.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Architectural moisture accent; combines with wild hydrangea, buttonbush, and ostrich ferns.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rain gardens, water garden borders, shaded moist borders, bioswales, and floral cutting gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
An essential woodland harbinger of spring, lighting up bare April woods with fragrant chartreuse-yellow flower clusters before leaves emerge. Foliage, twigs, and oval scarlet berries emit a tantalizing citrus-allspice aroma when crushed; leaves turn pure butter-yellow in fall.

Growth Habit & Form: Forms a broad, rounded, graceful understory shrub 6–12 ft tall and wide with smooth gray-brown bark.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Sole primary larval host plant for the magnificent Spicebush Swallowtail butterfly; dioecious (both sexes needed for berries).

Recommended Garden Settings: Woodland gardens, shaded stream banks, north/east foundation beds, and butterfly sanctuaries.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
Known as Rough Blazing Star, producing spectacular, stiff 2–4 ft vertical spires studded with large, rounded, button-like violet-purple flower heads with ruffled, crinkled bracts from August to October, blooming uniquely from top to bottom.

Growth Habit & Form: Erect, unbranched vertical wand 2–4 ft tall and 1–1.5 ft wide arising from a hard, drought-proof underground corm.

Sociability & Matrix Role: High-impact vertical monarch magnet; companions include little bluestem, goldenrods, and smooth blue aster.

Recommended Garden Settings: Prairie restorations, sunny perennial borders, dry sandy or rocky soils, and autumn showcase beds.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Thrives in dry, lean, sandy or rocky soils in full sun; exceptionally drought and heat resistant.
maintenance_guide.fall: Fluffy tan seedheads mature and feed American Goldfinches all autumn and winter.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stiff vertical spires stand erect through winter winds and snow.

advisor_description:
A tidy, historic native shrub producing fluffy, fragrant plumes of snowy-white blossoms resembling lilac panicles from June to July. Deep green serrated leaves were famously dried for 'Liberty Tea' during the American Revolution.

Growth Habit & Form: Compact, rounded shrub 2–3 ft tall and 3–5 ft wide with a massive, woody red taproot that defies drought.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Nitrogen-fixing prairie shrub; pairs with little bluestem, butterfly milkweed, and purple prairie clover.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, prairie restorations, dry rocky glades, and curbside hellstrips.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Extremely drought and heat tolerant once established; highly intolerant of poorly drained, soggy soils.
maintenance_guide.fall: Curious 3-lobed black seed capsules split explosively to disperse seeds.

advisor_description:
A magnificent aquatic native producing lush, glossy, heart-shaped or arrowhead-shaped emerald leaves up to 10 inches long, topped from June to September with dense, 3–6 inch spikes of intense violet-blue blossoms with yellow throat spots.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, clumping emergent aquatic perennial 2–4 ft tall and 2 ft wide spreading via thick, fleshy rhizomes in water.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Wetland and shoreline anchor; dragonflies perch on spikes; pairs with water lilies, arrowhead, and soft rush.

Recommended Garden Settings: Water gardens, retention pond shallows, rain garden retention basins, and wetland bog borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back dead foliage in early spring before fresh spears emerge through the water.
maintenance_guide.summer: Requires continuous saturated mud or standing water 2–12 inches deep in full sun for abundant flowering.
maintenance_guide.fall: Nutrient-rich seeds drop into water to feed migrating ducks and waterfowl.
maintenance_guide.winter: Ensure rhizomes are submerged below the winter ice freeze line in water gardens.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide fleshy rhizomes in late spring as active growth starts.

advisor_description:
An Ozark glade native producing erect to sprawling stems clothed in deeply lobed leaves, studded from late spring through summer with vibrant magenta, cup-shaped flowers that glow in the afternoon sun.

Growth Habit & Form: Forms an upright to sprawling clump 18–24 inches tall and 2–3 ft wide with a deep, drought-proof woody taproot.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Glade and border accent; interplants well with little bluestem, sideoats grama, and prairie dropseed.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dry rocky borders, limestone glades, rock gardens, and curbside hellstrips.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

Growth Habit & Form: Slender, upright perennial 1–2.5 ft tall that forms polite, airy colonies via slender underground rhizomes.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Late-season monarch caterpillar food and nectar source; fine texture pairs with little bluestem and purple coneflower.

Recommended Garden Settings: Prairie meadows, sunny borders, dry rocky glades, curbside hellstrips, and monarch waystations.

maintenance_guide.spring: Emerges in May; cut back old dried stems at 50°F+. Slow to show in spring, but thrives in heat.
maintenance_guide.summer: Virtually indestructible; laughs at severe drought, intense heat, poor rocky clay, and urban salt.

advisor_description:
A stunning, deep-rooted prairie legume displaying shimmering silvery-gray downy pinnate foliage topped in midsummer with dense 3–6 inch spikes of intense violet-blue flowers bristling with glowing golden-orange anthers.

Growth Habit & Form: Bushy subshrub 2–3 ft tall and 2 ft wide with an immense woody taproot penetrating up to 15 feet deep.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Nitrogen-fixing prairie keystone; companion to little bluestem, prairie dropseed, and compass plant.

Recommended Garden Settings: Prairie restorations, dry rocky glades, sunny borders, and low-water xeriscapes.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.
