maintenance_guide.spring: Cut stems back to 4–6 inches in spring (50°F+); regrows vigorously from woody crown.
maintenance_guide.summer: Immune to severe drought and heat; requires full sun and lean, sharply drained soil. Never fertilize.
maintenance_guide.fall: Silvery foliage turns golden-buff; small fuzzy seed pods feed native quail.
maintenance_guide.winter: Deep taproot enables survival through sub-zero Midwestern winters and prairie fires.

advisor_description:
An aristocratic, graceful prairie coneflower producing narrow, deeply drooping, ribbon-like pale pink to rose petals that dangle like shimmering fringe beneath an immense, bristly reddish-bronze central cone in June and July.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, slender perennial 2–3 ft tall and 1–1.5 ft wide arising from a massive, deep woody taproot.

Sociability & Matrix Role: High-impact early-summer prairie accent; blooms before purple coneflower; pairs with little bluestem and leadplant.

Recommended Garden Settings: Prairie restorations, dry sunny borders, limestone glades, rock gardens, and cutting borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
Known as Western Sunflower, this polite native produces mostly basal mounds of rough, oval leaves, sending up slender, almost naked 2–4 ft stems topped in late summer with cheerful, 2-inch bright yellow sunflower daisies.

Growth Habit & Form: Basal clump 2–4 ft tall and 1.5–2 ft wide with polite, short creeping rhizomes that do not overwhelm companions.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Well-behaved prairie sunflower; companions include little bluestem, purple prairie clover, and rough blazing star.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, prairie restorations, dry rocky glades, and pollinator meadows.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
Similar to A. arborea, offering spectacular early spring white blossom sprays, delicious June serviceberries, and radiant apricot-to-red fall foliage on a compact multi-stemmed form.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 15–25 ft tall and 10–15 ft wide with a dense, upright, suckering habit that forms a natural multi-stem grove.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Gregarious multi-stem accent; pairs beautifully with native dogwoods, viburnums, and seasonal woodland wildflowers.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rain gardens, pond edges, shrub borders, and bird habitat gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
An enchanting glade violet featuring deeply dissected, bird's-foot-like fan foliage, topped in April and May with large, velvety pansy-like blossoms with rich velvety dark violet upper petals and pale lilac lower petals with bright orange stamens.

Growth Habit & Form: Compact, tidy clump 3–6 inches tall and 6 inches wide with a thick, non-spreading rootstock.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Glade and rockery aristocrat; companion to prairie smoke, cedar sedge, and Missouri primrose.

Recommended Garden Settings: Limestone glades, dry sandy or gravelly slopes, rock garden crevices, and native trough planters.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Requires lean, sharply drained, acidic to neutral rocky or sandy soil in full sun to light shade; will rot in wet clay.
maintenance_guide.fall: Often reblooms lightly during cool autumn days.

advisor_description:
The exquisite 'Zigzag Goldenrod' featuring distinctive, sharply zig-zagging green stems clothed in broad, coarsely toothed, heart-shaped leaves, bearing bright golden-yellow flower clusters clustered in leaf axils from August to October.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, arching perennial 1.5–3 ft tall and 1.5 ft wide with short rhizomes forming polite, non-invasive clumps.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Shade matrix nectar engine; lights up dark woodland understories alongside heart-leaved aster and Christmas fern.

Recommended Garden Settings: Woodland shade gardens, shaded borders, north-facing slopes, and deciduous forest restorations.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
A colossal, ancient deciduous conifer featuring feathery, soft needle-like emerald foliage that turns rich coppery-cinnamon bronze before shedding in late autumn. Mature specimens in wet soil develop striking woody root 'knees'.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 50–70 ft tall with a 25–35 ft pyramidal spread. Highly adaptable, thriving equally in standing water or dry upland clays.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Stately architectural anchor; companion to river oats, swamp milkweed, and buttonbush in moist settings.

Recommended Garden Settings: Pond edges, rain gardens, stormwater retention basins, street tree lawns, and large open landscapes.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Remarkably drought tolerant once established despite wetland origin; root knees rarely form in well-drained upland lawns.
maintenance_guide.fall: Copper-orange fall foliage needles drop cleanly and form an excellent, weed-suppressing acidic mulch.

advisor_description:
A regal, architectural native fern producing giant, arching, feathery sterile fronds up to 4–5 ft tall resembling lush ostrich plumes. In late summer, rigid, dark woody fertile spikes emerge from the center, persisting through winter like decorative copper wands.

Growth Habit & Form: Forms bold, vase-like architectural colonies 3–5 ft tall and wide, spreading steadily by underground root runners in moist soil.

Sociability & Matrix Role: High-impact moisture matrix fern; pairs with wild hydrangea, buttonbush, and swamp milkweed.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rain gardens, shaded stream banks, moist woodland hollows, and foundation shade borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Medium Maintenance. Benefits from targeted mid-season care (such as Chelsea chopping or occasional division) and spring cutback timing to sustain peak vigor and compact garden form.
maintenance_guide.spring: Unfurling spring fiddleheads are famously harvested as gourmet wild edible greens in April. Clear dead fronds at 50°F+.
maintenance_guide.summer: Requires consistent moisture and shade; will scorch or go summer-dormant if allowed to dry out in hot sun.
maintenance_guide.fall: Feathery green fronds collapse after frost, leaving dark brown fertile fronds standing proud.
maintenance_guide.winter: Rigid, woody fertile fronds persist through winter snow, releasing spores onto the snowpack.
maintenance_guide.division: Vigorous spreader via stolons; dig and transplant running root runners in early spring.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
An unforgettable autumn sensation bearing dense, tight whorls of vivid iridescent magenta-purple berries wrapped around arching stems in September and October, accompanied by fuzzy lime-green leaves that turn yellow.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 3–6 ft tall and wide with an open, arching, loose vase form. Dies back to roots in harsh Midwestern winters.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Autumn focal point; companions include goldenrods, aromatic aster, and native switchgrass.

Recommended Garden Settings: Autumn showcase borders, bird habitat gardens, woodland edges, and sunny foundations.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Cut stems back to 4–6 inches from the ground in early spring (at 50°F+); blooms and fruits prolifically on new summer wood.
maintenance_guide.summer: Very drought and heat tolerant; thrives in average to dry soils in full sun to partial shade.
maintenance_guide.fall: Sensational neon-purple berries are eaten by over 40 songbird species; crushed leaves naturally repel mosquitoes.

advisor_description:
A rare, aristocratic native shade tree producing long, pendulous 10–15 inch wisteria-like panicles of intensely fragrant, creamy-white blossoms in late spring. Bright green pinnate leaves turn brilliant luminous gold in autumn, set against smooth beech-like gray bark.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 30–50 ft tall and 40–50 ft wide with a broad, graceful, rounded spreading canopy and smooth gray bark.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Specimen shade tree; deep root system allows lawn turf or shade perennials to flourish right up to the trunk.

Recommended Garden Settings: Lawn specimen, patio shade tree, native arboretum planting, and residential parkway.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
An unforgettable native woodland showstopper bearing upright clusters of tubular, 2-inch trumpet blossoms of intense flaming scarlet-red on the outside that flare open into five starry, chartreuse-yellow petals in June. The premier shade hummingbird flower.

Growth Habit & Form: Compact, upright clump 1–2 ft tall and 1.5 ft wide with fibrous roots and non-aggressive habit.

Sociability & Matrix Role: High-impact shade accent; pairs with wild hydrangea, maidenhair fern, and woodland phlox.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dappled shade gardens, woodland borders, shaded cottage beds, and hummingbird viewing borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Prefers rich, moist, well-drained organic soils in partial to full shade; can rebloom if deadheaded.
maintenance_guide.fall: Curious double-lobed seed capsules burst open to disperse seeds.

advisor_description:
A prostrate, trailing native prairie legume producing dense mats of small trifoliate leaves, studded from July to September with delicate, pea-like rose-purple to pink blossoms that trail softly along the ground.

Growth Habit & Form: Prostrate, mat-forming perennial 4–8 inches tall spreading 1.5–2.5 ft wide with a deep taproot.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Nitrogen-fixing living green mulch; pairs with little bluestem, sideoats grama, and prairie dropseed.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dry sunny slopes, erosion control, rock gardens, curbside hellstrips, and low-profile meadows.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
Known as Eastern Blazing Star or Large Blazing Star, producing magnificent, thick spires studded with large, rounded 1-inch violet-purple thistle buttons with distinctive ruffled bracts from August to October, blooming from the top downward.

Growth Habit & Form: Stately, upright wand 2–4 ft tall and 1.5 ft wide arising from a drought-hardy corm.

Sociability & Matrix Role: High-capacity monarch fueling station; companions include showy goldenrod, little bluestem, and switchgrass.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny borders, dry-to-medium prairie meadows, butterfly sanctuaries, and cutting gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Emerges late in spring; wait until 50°F+ before cutting back dried stems. Corms require sharp drainage.
maintenance_guide.summer: Very drought and heat tolerant; thrives in lean, well-drained loam or clay in full sun.
maintenance_guide.fall: Fluffy tan seed heads feed American Goldfinches all winter.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stout vertical stems stand strong in winter snow.
maintenance_guide.division: Separate offsets from mature corms in spring.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
The rare Missouri glade coneflower featuring drooping, ribbon-like rose-pink ray petals surrounding an architectural spiky coppery cone, distinguished botanically by emitting vibrant bright yellow pollen grains in June.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, slender perennial 2–3 ft tall and 1 ft wide with a deep, drought-proof woody taproot.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Glade specialist; companion to sideoats grama, Missouri evening primrose, and aromatic aster.

Recommended Garden Settings: Limestone glades, dry rocky borders, rock gardens, curbside hellstrips, and native show gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back old stalks at 50°F+, leaving 8–12 inches for stem-nesting bees.
maintenance_guide.summer: Thrives in thin, rocky, alkaline, baking limestone soils in full sun; impervious to drought.
maintenance_guide.fall: Spiky dark cones feed goldfinches and provide winter structure.
maintenance_guide.winter: Deep taproot survives sub-zero temperatures with ease.

advisor_description:
A magnificent late-summer native skullcap (cataloged as Scuttelaria incana) producing dense, branching panicles of rich violet-blue hooded tubular blossoms from July to September, held above soft, velvety downy-gray to green foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, bushy perennial 2–3 ft tall and 1.5–2 ft wide with a non-aggressive, polite fibrous root crown.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Late pollinator magnet; polite clump habit; pairs with wild bergamot, little bluestem, and black-eyed susans.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, open woodland edges, pollinator gardens, and cottage beds.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back old stems at 50°F+, leaving 8–12 inches for stem-nesting bees. Shoots emerge in April.
maintenance_guide.summer: Extremely drought and heat tolerant; thrives in dry-to-medium soils in full sun to partial shade.
maintenance_guide.fall: Curious helmet-like seed capsules rattle open; seeds feed songbirds.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stiff stems and calyx capsules provide subtle winter interest.

advisor_description:
A vigorous, luxuriant native wildlife powerhouse bearing massive 8–10 inch flat umbels of starry, fragrant white flowers in early summer, followed by heavy drooping clusters of glossy purple-black elderberries rich in antioxidants and vitamins.

Growth Habit & Form: Rapidly grows 8–12 ft tall and wide, forming a spreading, multi-stemmed, arching colonial shrub.

Sociability & Matrix Role: High-capacity wildlife resource; aggressive grower that thrives in moist boundary matrices alongside dogwoods and willows.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rain gardens, bioswales, edible homestead hedgerows, stream banks, and compost screen plantings.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Medium Maintenance. Benefits from targeted mid-season care (such as Chelsea chopping or occasional division) and spring cutback timing to sustain peak vigor and compact garden form.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back dead stems to the ground in early spring. Elderberries bloom on both old and new wood; a hard annual coppice keeps bushes compact and productive.
maintenance_guide.summer: Enjoys abundant moisture; mulch generously. Watch for ripe berries in August and protect with bird netting if harvesting for human syrup or wine.
maintenance_guide.fall: Berries are stripped clean by over 40 native bird species. Rake any diseased leaves.
maintenance_guide.winter: Hollow pithy stems provide prime winter nesting cavities for native solitary bees.
maintenance_guide.division: Easily divided in spring by digging rooted suckers; roots rapidly from hardwood cuttings.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A bountiful wildlife nut-bearing shrub featuring pendulous male catkins in late winter, broad heart-shaped green leaves that turn multi-colored copper, bronze, and red in fall, and delicious edible sweet native hazelnuts enclosed in ruffled papery bracts.

Growth Habit & Form: Reaches 8–12 ft tall and 6–10 ft wide with an upright, spreading habit, suckering to form dense defensive thickets.

Sociability & Matrix Role: High-value wildlife hedgerow anchor; host plant for numerous native moths and nesting cover for game birds.

Recommended Garden Settings: Edible native homestead plantings, windbreaks, property perimeter hedges, and woodland edges.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Prune out dead wood and thin oldest canes in late winter to maintain vigor and facilitate nut harvesting.
maintenance_guide.summer: Adaptable to a wide range of soils from clay to sand; drought tolerant once established.
maintenance_guide.fall: Harvest hazelnuts in September before blue jays and squirrels claim them; roast or eat fresh.
maintenance_guide.winter: Decorative 2–3 inch dangling male catkins provide kinetic winter beauty on bare twigs.
maintenance_guide.division: Dormant root suckers can be severed and transplanted in late autumn or early spring.

advisor_description:
A showstopping small tree draped in late spring with ethereal, fleecy clouds of fragrant, strap-like white petals resembling shredded fringe. Female plants produce clusters of dark blue olive-like fruits in late summer amid golden fall foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 12–20 ft tall and wide with a spreading, rounded multi-stemmed or single-stemmed framework. Slow growing.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Specimen accent; leaves emerge very late in spring, allowing early woodland spring ephemerals to bask in sunlight.

Recommended Garden Settings: Entryway gardens, shrub borders, foundation accents, and wildlife borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Be patient in spring—leaves emerge late (May). Prune lightly after bloom only if shaping is needed.
maintenance_guide.summer: Very pollution and urban tolerant; enjoys moist, rich, fertile soils but tolerates average clay.
maintenance_guide.fall: Dark blue drupes are quickly devoured by mockingbirds and bluebirds. Leaves turn clear bright yellow.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stout, coarse winter twigs with prominent buds; fully cold hardy.

advisor_description:
The 'Prairie Pussytoes', creating low, silvery-gray evergreen mats of small, narrow spoon-shaped leaves, sending up fuzzy 4–8 inch stems in early spring topped with charming, soft white kitten-paw flower heads.

Growth Habit & Form: Low, creeping stoloniferous groundcover 2–4 inches tall spreading 12–18 inches wide via surface runners.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Living silver mulch; larval host for American Lady butterfly; companions include prairie dropseed and blue grama.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dry sunny slopes, rock gardens, curbside hellstrips, glade borders, and path edging.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Pussy-toe flower stalks emerge early; caterpillars of American Lady butterflies web leaves into larval shelters.
maintenance_guide.summer: Immune to drought, heat, and poor, baking rocky soils; thrives where lawn grass burns out.
maintenance_guide.fall: Silvery foliage forms a tight, weed-proof mat that catches low autumn light.
maintenance_guide.winter: Evergreen silvery foliage provides year-round groundcover and winter soil erosion control.
maintenance_guide.division: Easily divided by digging rooted stolon runners in spring or autumn.

advisor_description:
A dramatic wetland emergent native bearing bold, architectural arrowhead-shaped glossy green leaves up to 12 inches long, topped in summer with whorled spikes of crisp, 3-petaled snowy-white blossoms with bright golden centers.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, clump-forming aquatic perennial 2–4 ft tall spreading via underwater stolons with edible starchy tubers.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Wetland wildlife resource; tubers famously known as 'Duck Potatoes'; pairs with blue pickerel and soft rush.

Recommended Garden Settings: Retention pond margins, water garden shallows, bioswales, rain garden basins, and marsh edges.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: High Maintenance. Requires active moisture management or boundary containment to manage vigorous growth. Adhere to seasonal timing to maximize ecological benefits while containing spread.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back dead foliage in early spring before fresh arrowhead leaves pierce the water.
maintenance_guide.summer: Requires constant saturated soil or standing water 2–12 inches deep in full sun to partial shade.
maintenance_guide.fall: Starchy underwater tubers swell in autumn, providing vital food for swans, ducks, and geese.
maintenance_guide.winter: Submerged tubers survive frozen winter mud safely.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide tubers in spring as active growth initiates.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A durable wetland legume shrub bearing dense 4–8 inch spires of deep purple-violet flowers with bright orange-gold stamens in early summer. Delicate pinnate locust-like foliage gives an airy, fine-textured appearance.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 6–10 ft tall and 8–12 ft wide with an open, vase-shaped spreading habit. Roots deeply to hold wet banks.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Nitrogen-fixing soil stabilizer; pairs with switchgrass, buttonbush, and swamp milkweed along shorelines.

Recommended Garden Settings: Riparian stream bank stabilization, pond edges, bioswales, and erosion control slopes.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back hard in early spring to encourage dense, bushy growth and prevent a leggy, bare-bottomed habit.
maintenance_guide.summer: Tolerates standing water, seasonal flooding, wind, poor alkaline soils, and heavy clay.
maintenance_guide.fall: Puckered, curved seed pods persist along stems; seeds feed waterfowl and quail.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stout woody stems catch flood debris and stabilize unstable waterway banks.
maintenance_guide.division: Propagate by stratified seed or semi-hardwood cuttings.

advisor_description:
A stunning, pendulous Missouri cliff native producing arching, cascading stems that spill over rocky ledges, covered in September and October with plume-like sprays of brilliant golden-yellow florets above velvety heart-shaped leaves.

Growth Habit & Form: Arching, cascading perennial 1.5–2.5 ft tall and wide with a woody rootstock adapted to rock crevices.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Cliff and rock wall specialist; pairs with aromatic aster, little bluestem, and fragrant sumac.

Recommended Garden Settings: Limestone glades, dry retaining walls, rock garden ledges, sunny slopes, and cascading borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
An essential early-season pollinator powerhouse bearing flat-topped umbels of tiny, brilliant golden-yellow florets in May and June, held above glossy, compound serrated foliage. An indispensable primary larval host for the Black Swallowtail butterfly.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, multi-stemmed clump 1.5–2.5 ft tall and 1.5 ft wide with non-aggressive fibrous roots.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Black Swallowtail nursery; pairs with prairie dropseed, columbine, and Ohio horsemint in moist borders.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rain gardens, moist meadows, sunny borders, woodland edges, and butterfly breeding sanctuaries.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Enjoys moist to medium soils in full sun to light shade; handles seasonal spring flooding with ease.
maintenance_guide.fall: Ribbed seed umbels turn purple-brown and feed ground-foraging birds; self-sows gently.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stout root crown is fully hardy under winter snow.

advisor_description:
A versatile 4-season small tree opening in late spring with abundant corymbs of snowy-white flowers, followed by lustrous maple-like leaves that turn dazzling orange, scarlet, and purple in fall, accompanied by clusters of long-lasting bright red winter berries.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 20–30 ft tall and 20–25 ft wide with a dense, rounded, thorny crown that provides superior bird nesting shelter.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Wildlife structural fortress; impenetrable thorny branches deter predators while flowers and fruit support birds and pollinators.

Recommended Garden Settings: Perimeter security borders, urban street lawns, wildlife thickets, and fall focal points.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

A low-growing warm-season marvel bursting in late summer with an ethereal, fluffy cloud of vivid reddish-purple inflorescences that hover like neon smoke over coarse green foliage, creating a mesmerizing visual haze.

Growth Habit & Form: Compact, tidy clumping grass 1–2 ft tall and wide, forming a rounded mound.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Front-of-border matrix filler; interplants seamlessly with Missouri evening primrose and butterfly weed.

Recommended Garden Settings: Hot, dry hellstrips, sandy or rocky soils, rock gardens, and massed sunny borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Thrives in the poorest, driest, most drought-parched rocky soils; full sun mandatory.
maintenance_guide.fall: Inflorescences detach in late autumn and roll across the ground like delicate purple tumbleweeds to disperse seed.
maintenance_guide.winter: Low rosette provides winter soil protection.
maintenance_guide.division: Easily divided in spring.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A charming, aromatic native known as 'Dittany', forming bushy mounds of mint-scented oval leaves covered in August and September with frothy clouds of tiny, two-lipped lavender to pale purple blossoms that buzz with tiny native bees.

Growth Habit & Form: Bushy, rounded subshrub-like clump 1–1.5 ft tall and wide with a woody base and fibrous roots.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Glade and rocky woodland edge matrix; companions include little bluestem, cliff goldenrod, and wild petunia.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dry rocky woods, limestone glades, rock gardens, path edging, and drought-tolerant borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back woody dead stems to 2 inches in early spring (at 50°F+); fresh aromatic shoots emerge in April.
maintenance_guide.summer: Extremely drought and rocky soil tolerant; thrives in poor, thin, well-drained acidic to alkaline soils.
maintenance_guide.fall: Famous for creating spectacular 'frost flowers' on the first freezing autumn nights as sap exudes from stems.
maintenance_guide.winter: Pearly ribbons of extruded ice curl around stem bases during early winter freezes.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide woody crowns in early spring.

advisor_description:
A fascinating, slow-growing understory botanical wonder blooming in very early spring with small, pendant bell-shaped lemon-yellow flowers before foliage. Notable for remarkably pliable, tough, leather-like twigs that can be tied in knots without breaking.

Growth Habit & Form: Compact, rounded understory shrub 3–6 ft tall and wide with a smooth, brown, tree-like miniature trunk.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Quiet woodland aristocrat; thrives in deep shade alongside maidenhair ferns and wild ginger.

Recommended Garden Settings: Shaded woodland gardens, native plant collector borders, ravine slopes, and contemplative paths.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Requires virtually no pruning. Allow natural miniature-tree form to develop slowly.
maintenance_guide.summer: Prefers moist, rich, organic, well-drained soils in dappled to full shade.
maintenance_guide.fall: Leaves turn clear, pale yellow before dropping cleanly in autumn.
maintenance_guide.winter: Unbelievably flexible, leathery twigs withstand heavy snow and ice without breaking.

advisor_description:
An exceptionally clean, rust-resistant native hawthorn celebrated for its peeling silvery-gray bark exposing orange inner wood, white late-spring flower clusters, and persistent glowing red winter berries that cling to bare branches through February.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 15–25 ft tall and wide with a vase-shaped to rounded, open, spreading branching habit. Has very few or small thorns.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Urban-tolerant understory tree; provides nesting cover and high-volume winter bird food.

Recommended Garden Settings: Street medians, urban courtyards, residential gardens, and naturalized bird havens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Prune lightly in late winter for structural clearance; highly resistant to foliar diseases.
maintenance_guide.summer: Thrives in heavy clay, drought, and temporary flooding; exceptionally tough Midwestern native.
maintenance_guide.fall: Foliage turns bronze to purple-red; clusters of red fruit ripen and persist through heavy snow.
maintenance_guide.winter: Peeling bark showing orange underbark combined with crimson fruit clusters is a winter showstopper.

advisor_description:
The iconic, rough-hairy Black-Eyed Susan bearing cheerful 2–3 inch golden-yellow daisy blossoms with domed chocolate-brown cones from June until frost, held on stiff, bristly stems with sandpapery green foliage.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, branched biennial/short-lived perennial 1–2.5 ft tall that self-sows prolifically to maintain permanent colonies.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Prolific pioneer wildflower; quickly fills bare soil in new prairie plantings, companioning with little bluestem.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny pollinator meadows, quick ground covers, cottage borders, hellstrips, and cutting gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Blooms continuously in full sun; virtually immune to drought and heat. Deadhead to prolong flowering.
maintenance_guide.fall: Allow late season seed cones to ripen; seeds feed goldfinches and perpetuate the colony for next year.

advisor_description:
Known as Palm Sedge for its unique, tropical-looking upright stems clothed in tiered whorls of pointed green leaves that resemble miniature palm trees, topped in summer with golden-brown seed spikes.

Growth Habit & Form: Grows 2–3 ft tall and 2 ft wide, forming a lush, upright, multi-stemmed colony via short rhizomes.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Textural moisture matrix; pairs with swamp milkweed, rose mallow, and Virginia sweetspire.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rain gardens, bioswales, wet borders, pond margins, and shaded foundation plantings.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
A robust, cool-season prairie and savanna grass producing dense, erect spike-like seed heads that resemble cultivated wheat or barley. Foliage emerges very early in spring with vibrant emerald green tones.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright clumping grass 2–4 ft tall and 1–2 ft wide with fibrous roots that establish quickly.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Early-season nurse grass; provides quick soil stabilization and ground cover for slower warm-season natives.

Recommended Garden Settings: Riparian buffer strips, wet-to-medium meadows, stream banks, and native revegetation.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back in late winter. Resumes active growth as soon as ground thaws in March.
maintenance_guide.summer: Often goes semi-dormant in midsummer heat; revives with autumn rains.
maintenance_guide.fall: Seed heads feed granivorous birds; leaves stay green late into autumn.
maintenance_guide.winter: Erect straw-colored stalks provide winter cover for ground wildlife.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide clumps in spring or fall.

advisor_description:
The queen of summer perennials, producing magnificent, fragrant domed panicles of sweet-scented rose-pink to magenta blossoms from July through September that act as a primary nectar source for tiger swallowtails and clearwing sphinx moths.

Growth Habit & Form: Stout, upright clump 3–4 ft tall and 2–3 ft wide with a dense fibrous root crown.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Back-of-border pollinator anchor; pairs with wild bergamot, switchgrass, and purple coneflower.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, cottage gardens, moist meadow plantings, and cutting gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Medium Maintenance. Benefits from targeted mid-season care (such as Chelsea chopping or occasional division) and spring cutback timing to sustain peak vigor and compact garden form.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back old stalks at 50°F+, leaving 8–12 inches of stubble for solitary bee nesting. Thin stems for airflow.
maintenance_guide.summer: Prefers rich, moist, organic soils in full sun; water at base to keep foliage dry and prevent powdery mildew.
maintenance_guide.fall: Deadhead spent flower panicles to encourage a secondary flush of late blooms in September.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stout stems hold upright; crowns survive deep winter cold under light compost mulch.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide mature clumps every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigorous center growth.

advisor_description:
An indispensable native evergreen groundcover forming dense, weed-choking mats of rounded, scalloped leathery leaves, erupting in April and May with cheerful clusters of bright golden-yellow daisy blossoms that illuminate shaded slopes.

Growth Habit & Form: Low, stoloniferous evergreen groundcover 4–6 inches tall (foliage) and 12–18 inches in bloom, spreading rapidly via runners.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Premier evergreen shade living mulch; companions include woodland phlox, columbine, and wild ginger.

Recommended Garden Settings: Woodland shade gardens, shaded erosion slopes, understory groundcover beneath trees, and path borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summer: Extremely adaptable; thrives in wet-to-dry soils in full shade to partial sun. Excellent weed suppressor.

advisor_description:
An Ozark glade native coneflower producing narrow, densely hairy foliage that defies baking heat, topped from July through October with starry golden-yellow daisy blossoms with domed blackish-brown central cones.

Growth Habit & Form: Stiff, upright clump 1–2 ft tall and 1 ft wide with a deep, drought-proof taproot.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Glade specialist; companions include glade coneflower, sideoats grama, and Missouri primrose.

Recommended Garden Settings: Limestone glades, dry rocky borders, rock gardens, curbside hellstrips, and low-water xeriscapes.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
The wild native ancestor of garden strawberries, producing runners lined with trifoliate toothed leaves, white 5-petaled flowers with golden centers in April and May, followed by intensely sweet, aromatic miniature wild red strawberries in June.

Growth Habit & Form: Low, creeping stoloniferous groundcover 4–7 inches tall spreading 12–24 inches wide via surface runners.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Edible living green mulch; suppresses weeds in sunny beds; companions include prairie dropseed and little bluestem.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny borders, orchard understory, edible native gardens, erosion control, and wildlife meadows.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

advisor_description:
Known as American Beakgrain, an attractive, bamboo-like woodland grass/wildflower producing broad, arching, lustrous green leaves up to 1 inch wide, topped in late summer with slender arching spikes bearing curious, beak-tipped shiny green-to-brown seeds.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, arching perennial 2–3 ft tall spreading slowly via short rhizomes into dense, weed-choking shade colonies.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Shade matrix groundcover; companions include wild hydrangea, black cohosh, and ostrich fern.

Recommended Garden Settings: Woodland gardens, shaded ravine banks, deciduous forest restorations, and shaded path borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

A magnificent native mountain mint featuring needle-fine, airy emerald foliage that looks like soft pine needles, topped from July to September with dense, flat-topped clusters of tiny white blossoms with purple specks. Leaves release an intense, invigorating peppermint aroma.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, bushy branched clump 2–3 ft tall and 2 ft wide with polite, slowly creeping rhizomes.

Sociability & Matrix Role: The undisputed #1 insect magnet in the garden—swarming with hundreds of beneficial pollinators, predatory wasps, and butterflies; polite clumper.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, prairie meadows, rain gardens, cottage beds, and herb gardens.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, clumping wetland perennial 2–3 ft tall and 1.5 ft wide spreading via creeping underground rhizomes.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Clear old dried foliage in early spring at 50°F+ before fresh green sword fans emerge.
maintenance_guide.summer: Prefers rich, moist to wet organic soils in partial shade; tolerates shallow standing water.
maintenance_guide.fall: Large 6-lobed seed capsules ripen and disperse corky seeds.
maintenance_guide.winter: Rhizomes overwinter safely under moist mulch or shallow water.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide crowded rhizomes in late summer after bloom every 3–4 years.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A refined, fine-textured cool-season bunchgrass bearing dense, narrow, silvery-green flower spikes in late spring that mature to glistening straw-colored seed heads. Silvery blue-green foliage stays compact and neat.

Growth Habit & Form: Tidy, upright clumping bunchgrass 1–2 ft tall and 1 ft wide with non-aggressive habit.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Early-season prairie matrix grass; pairs with blue-eyed grass, wild petunia, and lanceleaf coreopsis.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dry sunny borders, rock gardens, low-water meadows, and curbside hellstrips.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Comb out dead thatch or trim lightly in early spring before April bloom stalks emerge.
maintenance_guide.summer: Enjoys dry, well-drained, sandy to rocky soils; drought tolerant and low-growing.
maintenance_guide.fall: Foliage revives in cool autumn weather.
maintenance_guide.winter: Compact basal tuft remains neat through winter.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide in early spring or autumn.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
The undisputed 'King of the Prairie'—a towering, architectural grass producing distinctive 3-parted purple-and-bronze flower spikes resembling a wild turkey's foot. Foliage transitions from blue-green to radiant copper, burgundy, and orange in autumn.

Growth Habit & Form: Upright, commanding clumping bunchgrass 4–8 ft tall and 2–3 ft wide with a deep root system penetrating up to 12 feet deep.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Tallgrass matrix anchor; provides the structural backdrop for tall silphiums, sunflowers, and joe-pye weed.

Recommended Garden Settings: Large prairie restorations, sunny boundary screening, erosion stabilization, and wildlife corridors.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back in late spring at 50°F+. Highly adapted to spring prescribed prairie burns.
maintenance_guide.summer: Virtually indestructible once established; handles extreme drought, heat, wind, and heavy clay.
maintenance_guide.fall: Spectacular red-bronze autumn color; seeds feed small mammals and winter birds.
maintenance_guide.winter: Massive standing vertical architecture catches snowdrifts and shelters wildlife.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide large clumps with a mattock or sharp spade in spring.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
A show-stopping native wetland mallow producing colossal, saucer-shaped 6–8 inch blossoms of creamy-white with a deep velvety crimson-wine eye and prominent yellow stamen column from July through September, set against large, velvety heart-shaped leaves.

Growth Habit & Form: Stout, multi-stemmed shrub-like clump 4–6 ft tall and 3–4 ft wide that dies completely to the ground in winter.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Dramatic moisture anchor; specialist host for native Hibiscus Turret Bees; pairs with buttonbush and rose mallow.

Recommended Garden Settings: Rain gardens, retention pond margins, bioswales, wet drainage ditches, and sunny moist borders.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: High Maintenance. Requires active moisture management or boundary containment to manage vigorous growth. Adhere to seasonal timing to maximize ecological benefits while containing spread.
maintenance_guide.spring: Emerges very late in spring (late May) from rootstock; mark location. Cut old woody canes back to 6 inches at 50°F+.
maintenance_guide.summer: Requires full sun and consistent moisture; thrives in heavy saturated clay and shallow standing water.
maintenance_guide.fall: Hairy seed capsules mature and split; seeds feed waterfowl and marsh birds.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stout woody canes provide winter architectural interest; rootstock is completely winter hardy.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide massive root crowns in early spring with a sharp spade.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
The magnificent 'Culver's Root' sending up stately, architectural spires topped in July and August with elegant, candelabra-like branched wands of tiny, creamy-white to pale blush florets that open from the base upward, held above clean tiered whorls of lance-shaped leaves.

Growth Habit & Form: Stately, upright columnar clump 3–5 ft tall and 2–3 ft wide with a deep, non-aggressive root crown.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Architectural vertical accent; premier butterfly and bumblebee flower; pairs with Joe-Pye weed and switchgrass.

Recommended Garden Settings: Sunny perennial borders, prairie meadows, rain gardens, cottage backdrops, and pollinator plantings.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Medium Maintenance. Benefits from targeted mid-season care (such as Chelsea chopping or occasional division) and spring cutback timing to sustain peak vigor and compact garden form.
maintenance_guide.spring: Cut back dried stalks at 50°F+, leaving 12 inches for stem-nesting bees. Shoots emerge with red tints in May.
maintenance_guide.summer: Thrives in moist to medium, well-drained soils in full sun; provide supplemental water during extreme drought.
maintenance_guide.fall: Candelabra flower spikes mature to rich chocolate-brown seed wands; do not cut back in autumn.
maintenance_guide.winter: Stout candelabra silhouettes provide mesmerizing vertical winter drama in snowdrifts.
maintenance_guide.division: Divide mature crowns in early spring every 4–5 years.
maintenance_guide.sources: Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Sow Wild Natives

advisor_description:
Stunning small tree featuring extremely glossy, leathery dark emerald leaves with rusty-velvety undersides and buds. Clusters of pure white spring flowers give way to pruinose blue-black berries and brilliant crimson-purple fall color.

Growth Habit & Form: Reaches 10–18 ft with a dense, rounded, sturdy framework. Exceptional drought and limestone tolerance.

Sociability & Matrix Role: Architectural specimen for dry or sunny areas; pairs with aromatic sumac and little bluestem.

Recommended Garden Settings: Dry limestone glades, upland borders, specimen lawn accents, and heat-exposed perimeters.

Sources: Missouri Botanical Garden PlantFinder, Grow Native! (Missouri Prairie Foundation), Sow Wild Natives, City Roots Nursery, MDC.

maintenance_guide.summary: Low Maintenance. Requires minimal care once established. Follow ecological cutback practices to protect native pollinators and songbirds.
maintenance_guide.spring: Prune dead wood in early spring; shape lightly after bloom if necessary.
maintenance_guide.summer: Remarkably drought tolerant once roots take hold; thrives in tough rocky clays.
maintenance_guide.fall: Glossy leaves turn luminous ruby-red; berries persist into early winter for wildlife.
maintenance_guide.winter: Rusty-velvet flower buds and deeply fissured blocky dark bark.
maintenance_guide.division: Propagate by seed; do not divide established taproot.
